analysis.one_liner: Caps national health spending and provider payments while expanding coverage to children, seniors, and low-income families.
analysis.headline: Referred to three House committees the day it was introduced and never taken up again; the bill died without a single hearing, markup, or vote when the 103rd Congress ended in January 1995.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have put an annual cap on total national health spending, limited what hospitals and doctors could charge both government programs and private insurers, and required all health plans to meet federal standards including community rating. At the same time it would have expanded Medicaid eligibility, added preventive care and prescription drug coverage to Medicare, created a health insurance program for all children under 19, and cracked down on health care fraud and physician self-referral.
analysis.who_benefits: Ordinary patients and the uninsured. Children under 19 would get coverage through a new federal program; Medicare beneficiaries would gain prescription drug, mammography, colon cancer screening, and immunization benefits; low-income people would gain Medicaid eligibility; and everyone with insurance would benefit from slower premium growth if national spending caps held costs down. Small employers and the self-employed would gain a permanent, larger health insurance deduction.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Uninsured children, seniors, and low-income families

how_it_helps.text: Creates a national health expenditure budget beginning in 1995 whose allowed growth shrinks each year until it matches economic growth, to slow the rise of health costs and premiums.

Lets states set payment rates for hospital and physician services across all payers, and sets federal maximum payment rates in states that do not, so providers could no longer shift costs between public and private patients.
Requires every health benefit plan to be certified against federal standards, including community-rated premiums and guaranteed issuance and renewal, backed by an excise tax on non-compliant plans.
Makes all children under 19 eligible for a health insurance program with benefits generally matching Medicare's, plus well-child care.

Expands Medicaid eligibility for low-income people with full federal payment for the new costs, and adds Medicare coverage of annual mammography, colon cancer screening, child immunizations, well-child care, and outpatient prescription drugs.
Extends the ban on physician self-referrals to all payers and strengthens fraud and abuse enforcement, including treble damages, to reduce wasteful spending.

analysis.who_pays: Hospitals and physicians would bear the largest cost, since the bill caps what they can charge and collect from every payer, not just Medicare. Prescription drug makers would face Medicare drug coverage priced under a new payment methodology. Health insurers would have to meet certification standards and community rating, and providers would face new reporting duties under the national health expenditure reporting system.

drawbacks.text: National maximum payment rates applied to all payers were untested at this scale; if rates were set too low, providers could reduce services, and the bill's own assurances on hospital access relied on Secretary enforcement and civil money penalties as small as $100 per improper charge.

The bill creates a heavy administrative apparatus — a national budget, service classes, provider reporting, uniform claims cards, and electronic reporting — whose compliance costs would fall on providers and plans, and the increase in allowed spending above GDP growth was phased to zero after 1998, leaving little room for medical innovation or new technology.
The bill preempts state 'any willing provider' laws and steers coverage through managed care and new health plan purchasing cooperatives, which could limit some patients' choice of doctor.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The coverage expansions — children's insurance, Medicaid growth, and Medicare drug and preventive benefits — are concrete and would have reached millions of people. The centerpiece cost controls traded that certainty against real risk: capping every provider's revenue from every payer was the most aggressive version of cost control proposed in this era, and its effects on access and quality depended entirely on how the Secretary set rates. The design was also very complex, which made it hard to enact even before any interest group opposition is counted.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to three House committees at introduction and then to subcommittees, but no committee ever held a markup and it never reached the floor; it died when the 103rd Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. Pete Stark introduced the Health Care Cost Containment and Reform Act on January 5, 1993, the opening day of the 103rd Congress.
It was referred jointly to three committees — Ways and Means, Energy and Commerce, and Education and Labor — and within weeks sent to health and related subcommittees in each.
No committee action followed. The only later entries in the action history are the sponsor's introductory remarks in the Congressional Record in April, May 1993 and February 1994.
The bill never received a markup, a floor vote in either chamber, or any roll call, and it expired when the Congress ended on January 3, 1995.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Hospitals, physicians, and insurers were better off because the bill died: none of the all-payer payment caps, the national health budget, or the plan certification and community-rating requirements ever took effect. Children, Medicare beneficiaries, and low-income people lost the coverage expansions that died with it.

sides.party_line_note: The bill never reached a vote, so no roll call shows the divide; its sponsor and all three cosponsors were House Democrats, and the three committee chairmen who never acted were also Democrats.

industries.note: The bill capped what hospitals could charge and collect from all payers, private and public, using Medicare-style payment rates, with states allowed to run their own all-payer rate systems instead. Hospital revenue growth would have been constrained by the national health budget, which is why this industry's interest ran against the bill's cost savings for patients and taxpayers.

Physician payments would have been capped under a maximum fee schedule applied to every payer, and the ban on physician self-referrals would have extended beyond Medicare to all payers and additional services.

Plans would face federal certification, an excise tax for non-compliance, and community-rated premiums, but the bill also channels coverage through private plans and new health plan purchasing cooperatives. The dominant effect for insurers was regulation they opposed; the coverage expansions depended on their continued role as the delivery channel.

industries.industry: Health maintenance organizations and managed care
industries.note: The bill repeals the sunset on HMO dual-choice requirements, preempts state any-willing-provider laws, funds new staff and group model HMOs with federal grants, and exempts staff/group HMOs from the payment caps, locking managed care in as the main vehicle for cost containment.

Medicare would cover outpatient prescription drugs, with payment determined using Medicare drug payment methods and a new Prescription Drug Payment Review Commission reporting on drug payment methods, creating government pressure on drug prices.
